What You’d Notice Picking This Up Cold

Item B2 is a small gold-coloured hex nut. Look at one face and you’ll see a ring of whitish nylon set into the top of the threaded hole — that ring is what makes it a lock nut.

The 3D model shows the profile: a hex body with a rounded collar on top, where the nylon insert sits.
The same shape on the DIN 985 drawing. The hatched area in the side view is the nylon insert, labelled “prevailing torque element”.

Hex Body

Six flat sides let a wrench or socket turn the nut. Their width is the “width across flats” (see ).

Nylon Insert

A nylon ring at the top of the nut grips the bolt threads so the nut resists loosening (see ).

Brass, Plain

Small M4 Thread

An internal M4 coarse thread with a 0.7 mm pitch, called out by the “4C” in the part number.

Topic T3 · Standard & Specification

The Full Item Specification

DIN 985 nylon-insert lock nuts, in one reference table.

Measurement System
The DIN 985 drawing: the nut in side and plan views. According to the part number, every dimension on it is in millimeters.

Metric

The part number tells you the system before you read anything else: the leading “.” and the “M” both mean metric, following the SBS part number structure standard.

Standard / Type
DIN 985, page 1 — title, field of application and dimension drawing (click to enlarge). Read the full DIN 985 standard ↗

DIN 985

This part is made to DIN 985: prevailing torque type hexagon thin nuts with nonmetallic insert. The standard sets the shape and the size limits for the nut, including the three dimensions you will measure in .

It covers sizes M3 to M48: product grade A up to M16, product grade B above.

Withdrawn, Still on the Print
The DIN 985 entry in the SBS Standards Library: status Withdrawn, replaced by DIN EN ISO 10511. Search the Standards Library ↗

DIN 985 → ISO 10511

DIN 985 has been withdrawn and replaced by DIN EN ISO 10511. Withdrawn does not mean the part disappears: the item description, the customer’s print and the SBS inspection report for .4CMLNB all still call out DIN 985.

If a customer asks for the ISO number, ISO 10511 is the one to look at — but always confirm against their print before treating the two as interchangeable.

Topic T4 · Material & Grade

Brass

The material tells you what the nut is made of and what it’s good at. Here’s what brass means on the shop floor.

Requirement

Material: brass · Grade: brass

Material: Brass

Brass is an alloy of copper and zinc. It is the “B” at the end of the part number and the word BRASS at the end of the description.

Grade

For a brass nut the grade field simply repeats the material. There is no steel strength class (like the “CL 8” on a steel nut) to look for.

The gold colour is the brass itself, not a coating.
Why Brass Instead of Steel

Won’t Rust

Brass contains no iron, so it does not rust. It can darken or tarnish over time, but it does not need a plating to protect it.

Non-Magnetic

Brass is not attracted to a magnet — useful near compasses, sensors and electronics.

Conducts Electricity

Copper-based alloys carry current well, so brass hardware turns up on electrical terminals and grounding points.

Lower Strength

Brass is softer and weaker than steel. It is chosen for its corrosion and electrical properties, not to carry heavy clamp loads.

What DIN 985 Says

DIN 985 defaults to the nut materials of DIN 267 Part 15. When a different material is used — such as brass — the standard says it shall be agreed at the time of ordering. That agreement is why the material is spelled out on the description and checked on the inspection report ().

Topic T5 · Surface Finish

Plain — No Finish

Some parts have a coating, plating or treatment added after they are made. This one doesn’t.

Requirement

None. This piece has no finish, so it remains plain.

In the Part Number

There is no finish suffix after the “B” — a plain part simply ends at the material code.

What You See

The natural gold surface of the brass, with nothing applied on top. The nylon ring is a separate part of the nut, not a finish.

The nuts as supplied: plain brass, no coating.
Why No Finish Is Needed
  • Brass does not rust, so it does not need the zinc plating a steel nut would get.
  • A plating on top of the brass would add thickness to the threads and the nylon insert would still need to grip cleanly.
  • The finish field still matters: “Plain” is what the item specification and the description expect, so a plated nut would not match.

Topic T6 · Thread & Nut Type

M4-0.7 Coarse Nylon-Insert Lock Nut

The “4”, “C” and “LN” in the part number describe the thread and the kind of nut.

Thread
The side view marks the thread diameter d. The inspection report calls the thread out as M4-.7 6H.

Thread: M4-0.7

The internal thread of this nut is an M4 size thread — 4 mm nominal diameter, the “4” in the part number. 6H is the tolerance class for the internal thread.

Thread Pitch & Thread Type
DIN 985 table, row P (marker 4): the M4 pitch is 0.7 mm.

0.7 mm Pitch

The thread pitch of this part is 0.7 mm.Pitch: the distance from one thread crest to the next.

Coarse

The thread type is coarse — the “C” in the part number. DIN 985’s footnote says P is the coarse pitch from DIN 13, and 0.7 mm is the coarse pitch for M4.Coarse thread: fewer, deeper threads per length than a fine thread.

Nut Type: Hex, Thin, Nylon Insert

Hex

The nut type is hex, named for its six-sided shape.

Lock Nut (LN)

“LN” in the part number marks a lock nut; the description spells it out as NYLON INS LKNUT.

Thin

DIN 985 is the thin version of the nylon-insert nut: for M4 the overall height is only 5 mm.

Prevailing Torque

A nut that needs turning effort all the way on, even before it is tight, is called a prevailing torque nut. The nylon insert is what creates that effort.

How the Nylon Insert Locks

Prevailing Torque Element

  1. An unthreaded ring. A nylon ring sits in a collar at the top of the nut. Its hole is slightly smaller than the bolt.
  2. The bolt forms its own thread. As the bolt is turned through, it presses a thread into the nylon.
  3. The nylon grips back. The nylon pushes against the bolt threads, creating friction that resists turning.
  4. It holds under vibration. That grip keeps the nut from backing off when the assembly shakes.

3D model of a brass nylon-insert lock nut in cutaway, built to M4 proportions (7 mm across flats, 5 mm tall). The white ring is the nylon insert, held in by the swaged lip of the top collar. DIN 985 leaves the exact design to the manufacturer.
Nylon Insert vs. All-Metal Lock Nut
Nylon insertAll-metalDrag to rotate

The 3D view needs WebGL, which this browser has turned off.

Two ways to lock a nut, cut away on a steel bolt. Left: the white nylon insert grips the thread. Right: the top of the all-metal nut is squeezed out of round, so the metal itself grips the thread.

Nylon Insert

The white ring grips the bolt thread. This is the type of lock nut in this module, built to DIN 985.

All-Metal

No plastic: the top of the nut is deformed so the metal grips the thread. Often chosen when heat is a concern.

Checking the Thread with a Plug Gauge

Go / No-Go Plug Gauge (M4-0.7 6H)

  1. Two ends, two jobs. A plug gauge has a GO end and a NO GO end.
  2. GO end: it must pass into the thread. If it does, the thread is correct.
  3. NO GO end: it must not pass into the thread.
  4. If the results differ from this, the piece must be rejected.

Topic T7 · Measuring the Nut

Three Dimensions, One Caliper

Three letters on the DIN 985 drawing — s, e and h — give the limits for checking the nut, and each can be measured with a caliper. The limits come from the DIN 985 table in .

s = width across flats, e = width across corners, h = overall height, as drawn in DIN 985. m is the minimum thread length and m′ the minimum wrenching height.
Limits & Caliper Check

Width Across Flats (s)

Min 6.78 mm / Max 7.00 mm
DIN 985, M4 column, s rows: max = nominal size 7, min 6.78.

Width Across Corners (e)

Min 7.66 mm
DIN 985, M4 column, e row. There is no maximum to check.

Height (h)

Min 4.70 mm / Max 5.00 mm
DIN 985, M4 column, h rows: max = nominal size 5, min 4.7.

Where the numbers come from: DIN 985 table, M4 column. Markers 1–3 are the three caliper checks. Read the full DIN 985 standard ↗

Measuring Tips

Measure s across two opposite flats and e across two opposite corners. Measure h from the bearing face to the top of the nylon collar — the collar is part of the height.

A reading inside the min/max is a pass. Remember to zero the caliper first; at this size a 0.1 mm error matters.

Topic T8 · Applications

Where This Nut Gets Used

Brass and a nylon insert make this nut a fit for wet, electrical and vibrating assemblies.

Marine & Powersports

Brass resists corrosion around water and salt air — and this item carries a cross-reference to a BRP part number.

Electrical

Terminal blocks, grounding studs and panels, where a non-magnetic, conductive nut is wanted.

Electronics & Instruments

Small M4 hardware near sensors, compasses or magnets, where steel would interfere.

Plumbing & Fittings

Wet locations where a steel nut would rust.

What the Nylon Insert Adds
  • Resists loosening under vibration, without a separate lock washer or thread-locking compound.
  • Holds its position even before it is fully tightened, thanks to the prevailing torque.
  • Stays in one piece — the locking feature is built into the nut, so there is nothing extra to lose.
Where It’s Not the Right Choice

High Temperature

DIN 985 notes that performance at temperatures above +120 °C must be agreed at ordering — the nylon softens with heat.

Yield-Point Tightening

DIN 985 states these nuts are not suitable for yield-point tightening methods.

Reference

Glossary

Every code, acronym, and standard used in this module, defined in plain language. Tap a term’s “jump” button to see it in context.

Brass

An alloy of copper and zinc. It does not rust, is non-magnetic and conducts electricity, but is weaker than steel. The “B” at the end of the part number.

Coarse Thread

A thread with fewer, deeper threads per length than a fine thread. For M4 the coarse pitch is 0.7 mm.

Customer Part Number

A customer’s own number for the same item, cross-referenced on the SBS site. For this part: BRP part # 232541200.

DIN 985

The German standard for prevailing torque type hexagon thin nuts with nonmetallic (nylon) insert. Published 1987, now withdrawn but still called out on this part’s description and inspection report.

DIN EN ISO 10511

The standard that replaced DIN 985 for thin nylon-insert lock nuts.

Go / No-Go Plug Gauge

A thread gauge with two ends: the GO end must enter the thread and the NO GO end must not. Any other result rejects the part.

Height (h)

The overall height of the nut, nylon collar included. For this part: minimum 4.70 mm, maximum 5.00 mm.

Inspection Report

The filled-in copy of the inspection template, recording the measured dimensions and the pass/fail evaluation for a lot.

Inspection Template

The blank, controlled form that defines how the part is checked. For this item it is linked in P21 under Document Links.

Lock Nut (LN)

A nut designed to resist loosening. “LN” in the part number marks this category.

M4-0.7

The thread size: 4 mm nominal diameter with a 0.7 mm pitch. 6H is the tolerance class of the internal thread.

Metric

The measurement system for this part. Both the leading “.” and the “M” in the part number mean metric.

Nylon Insert

A nylon ring in the top of the nut. The bolt forms a thread in it, and the nylon’s grip keeps the nut from backing off.

P21

The SBS ERP system. Item Maintenance holds the item’s inspection, lot-tracking and document-link settings.

Plain Finish

No plating or coating; the part is left as the bare material. Shown by the absence of a finish code after the “B”.

Prevailing Torque

Turning effort needed to run a nut down the bolt even before it is tight, created here by the nylon insert.

Thread Pitch

The distance between neighbouring threads, in millimeters for a metric part. This nut: 0.7 mm.

VMI (Vendor-Managed Inventory)

A bin system where SBS manages and restocks parts directly at the customer’s location. This training module is named after Item B2’s cell on the VMI bin card (column B, row 2).

Width Across Corners (e)

The distance between two opposite corners of the hexagon, identified with the letter e. For this part: minimum 7.66 mm.

Width Across Flats (s)

The distance between two opposite flat sides of the hexagon, identified with the letter s. For this part: minimum 6.78 mm, maximum 7.00 mm.
